speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. I see you are an 8-month-old boy with feeding difficulties and abdominal distension. To help me understand your symptoms better, tell me: have you noticed any vomiting, and if so, is it forceful or projectile?

speaker: Patient
text: The baby has been very fussy, feeding less than usual, and the abdomen looks distended. Crying gets worse when the belly is touched.

speaker: Doctor
text: That sounds very painful for him. Does the baby also have episodes of drawing their knees up to their chest or passing stool that looks like "currant jelly"? Also, has any green (bilious) fluid come out when he vomits?

speaker: Patient
text: There has not been fever, vomiting, or diarrhea like a stomach infection. The baby was born at 39 weeks without birth complications.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for clarifying; the absence of fever, vomiting, or diarrhea helps rule out simple gastroenteritis. Since the abdomen is painful to touch and distended, could you describe the exact location of the pain and whether the baby has passed any stool or gas today?

speaker: Patient
text: The baby did not seem to pass stool normally and the belly swelling has become more obvious. Feeding has clearly decreased over the past few days.

speaker: Doctor
text: The lack of stool passage combined with progressive distension and feeding difficulty suggests an obstruction. Have you noticed any "sausage-shaped" masses in the abdomen, or has the belly become tender to the touch? REQUEST TEST: Abdominal_X-Ray. REQUEST IMAGES.

speaker: Doctor
text: The X-ray showing dilated bowel with an absent rectal gas pattern confirms a distal obstruction. Given the infant's age and the severity of the distension, is there any history of a polyhydramnios pregnancy (excess amniotic fluid) or failure to pass meconium within the first 48 hours of life?

speaker: Patient
text: The abdomen still looks swollen and the baby seems uncomfortable, especially in the lower abdomen.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Distal Intestinal Obstruction (likely Jejunal or Ileal Atresia).

The clinical picture of progressive abdominal distension, obstipation (no stool), and the X-ray finding of dilated bowel with a gasless rectum strongly confirms a distal obstruction. I will proceed with surgical consultation immediately to plan for exploratory laparotomy.
